AI chipmaker Nvidia (NASDAQ: $NVDA) is preparing to oust founder and CEO Jensen Huang after reports that he had two extramarital affairs, the Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter. The company hasn't confirmed the report. The Journal said directors could meet as soon as Wednesday to decide Huang's future. Nvidia shares fell about 8% in after-hours trading on the report. The company's chips sit at the center of the AI infrastructure being built by CoreWeave (NASDAQ: $CRWV) and by Bitcoin (CRYPTO: $BTC) miners moving into AI computing. According to the Journal, one of the relationships was with a woman U.S. officials reportedly suspect of having ties to Chinese intelligence. Huang acknowledged an affair in a message to staff on Sunday, apologizing for violating his wife's trust, as the board investigates whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The New York Times reported earlier Wednesday that he also had a relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, citing a video it said was taken at a San Jose hotel in March. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Journal's report, and Reuters said it could not immediately verify it. Beijing has dismissed the spying allegations. The reports have drawn scrutiny from lawmakers and investors over Huang's conduct and over Nvidia's lack of a succession plan. Nvidia has not named a candidate to replace him. Huang co-founded the company in 1993, and it has a market value above $4 trillion. Shares of Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) are down 7.28% at $161.08 in after hours trading. CNBC's Jim Cramer lamented the spectacular downfall of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, declaring that the scandal engulfing the tech giant made the infamous Theranos debacle "look like child's play." Cramer delivered his blistering assessment on Wednesday's edition of Mad Money, just after The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia's board was preparing to oust Huang amid revelations about his alleged affairs with a company executive and a suspected Chinese spy. The CNBC host called the news out of Nvidia "hideous" following the "big blue wave" that swept Democrats into power in last week's midterm elections. Referencing "the heartbreak of an Nvidia possibly without Jensen Huang," Cramer admitted, "All things considered, I would rather be in Colgate or Johnson & Johnson." "The greatest investing story ever told became almost overnight a blight on our country, with its chief spokesperson caught up in some tawdry spy scandal that made Theranos look like child's play," he said, adding that there was "another revelation tonight — Jensen's a goner." The Journal reported Wednesday evening that Nvidia's board was preparing to meet as soon as that day to decide on Huang's future at the company. The report followed another bombshell from The New York Times, which revealed that Huang allegedly had a previously undisclosed relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care. The mounting scandal has also triggered bipartisan outrage in Washington, where lawmakers are demanding accountability from the embattled executive. Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-ND) called for Huang's resignation earlier Wednesday, warning on CNBC that the CEO was vulnerable to "extortion" and "blackmail" because of his alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. "I can't believe we are even considering him not resigning," the senator said. His position put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who has so far continued to defend Huang, calling him a "very honorable guy." Nvidia's stock price tumbled after the close of trading on Wednesday on news that the chipmaker's board of directors is preparing to oust longtime CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia this week launched an investigation into Huang, who admitted to having an extramarital affair. U.S. intelligence agencies have linked the CEO to a Chinese business executive, Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security. The Trump administration is aware of the Nvidia board's plans, sources told CBS News. The Wall Street Journal was the first to report that board members were preparing to remove Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares fell more than 8%, to $159.51, in after-hours trading. The drop continued a steep decline in the company's market value, which has sunk more than $450 billion since Nvidia announced the probe into Jensen Huang's conduct on Nov. 8. Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, is seen in many circles as the face of the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector, with the company's advanced chips providing the critical computing resources that power frontier AI models. His departure would be a major blow to Nvidia, which lacks any obvious successor to fill his shoes, according to Wall Street analysts. "The news is obviously negative, as Jensen is (arguably) the most prominent executive at the most prominent company sitting at the center of the world's most important industry — someone who foresaw the rise of AI years before ChatGPT arrived and made sure the firm he founded would be prepared to capitalize on it," Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge said in a report. Corporate governance experts said Jensen Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang appears to violate Nvidia's code of conduct. That policy highlights that personal relationships could create a conflict of interest for Nvidia, while Huang himself specifies in the code of conduct that the company's workers have a responsibility "to maintain high ethical standards." Nvidia's code also instructs employees to ask themselves whether they could defend an action if it were made public on social media or known to colleagues. If not, the policy states, "do not proceed." In a message to company employees on Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair, and he apologized to his wife and their two children, both of whom also work at Nvidia. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote. Nvidia's 11-person board includes Jensen Huang, although the other board members are designated as independent, according to a regulatory filing. President Trump said this week the FBI is also investigating romantic and business ties between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who was a senior executive at Megaspeed International. The Singapore-based company has been one of Nvidia's largest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and other advanced hardware. The turmoil at Nvidia is also drawing scrutiny in Congress, with lawmakers expected to question company executives about whether its chips are being funneled to China through other countries. Dan Ives, a tech analyst with investment adviser Yorkville Ives, said investors will now consider who might succeed Huang, what impact that could have on the company's short-term strategy and what any government investigations might reveal. "Jensen is not replaceable by another CEO or group of interim executives, but Nvidia likely now has to move on without Jensen at the helm, which seemed like a Twilight Zone episode narrative before Sunday afternoon when the news broke," Ives said in a report. A relationship with a direct report turns the board's problem into one that boards have handled before, and twice in the past decade the CEO had to go. Here is what happened to shareholders those two times. On June 21, 2018, Intel said CEO Brian Krzanich had resigned after an investigation found a past consensual relationship with an employee, which broke a company policy that applied to managers. Intel had no successor ready. Chief financial officer Bob Swan ran the company as interim CEO for seven months before the board gave him the job in January 2019, while Intel was also struggling to get its next generation of chips into production. Intel stock fell 2.4% that day, counting from the prior close, while the S&P 500 fell 0.6%. A year later, with dividends counted, Intel was down 8.7% while the S&P 500 was up 8.5%, a gap of 17 percentage points. On Sunday, November 3, 2019, McDonald's said its board had fired CEO Steve Easterbrook for a consensual relationship with an employee, which violated company policy. The board named Chris Kempczinski, who ran the U.S. business, as CEO in the same announcement. In August 2020 the company sued Easterbrook, saying he had hidden other relationships, and in 2021 he agreed to return more than $105 million in pay. McDonald's stock fell 2.7% the next trading day. A year later, with dividends counted, it was up 14.7%, ahead of the S&P 500's 11.9%, even with the 2020 crash in between. Six months in, during that crash, both McDonald's and the index were down: 7.6% and 6.1%. The first-day drops were small in both cases, under 3%. Nvidia has already fallen more than that after hours tonight alone. What separated the two outcomes came later, and it was mostly about two things: whether the board had a successor ready on day one, and whether the business underneath was healthy. McDonald's had both. Intel had neither, and its stock lagged for the year that followed. Nvidia has no named successor. "Mr. Huang being removed immediately could be challenging for Nvidia since it does not have a succession plan in place," Gil Luria of D.A. Davidson told Reuters after the Journal's report. Huang co-founded the company in 1993 and has run it ever since, which makes him harder to replace than Krzanich or Easterbrook, who were both hired managers. Nvidia's early mover's advantage enabled it to dominate the AI data center market with its chips, and it locks in those customers with its proprietary software and services. From fiscal 2021 to fiscal 2026 (which ended this January), Nvidia's revenue grew from $16.7 billion to $215.9 billion, while its net income jumped from $4.3 billion to $120.1 billion. Over the past year, the Iran war, inflation, and the Fed's interest rate hike in September drove more investors to question that bullish thesis. As the costs of building new data centers outpaced the monetization of new AI services, it became harder to justify those expenses. The Democratic sweep of the midterm elections on Nov. 3 exacerbated that pressure. Several newly elected officials -- including Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa -- have called for moratoriums on new data centers until tighter regulations are rolled out. On Nov. 8, Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang admitted that he had an extramarital affair in a public company memo. Several reports also called Alice Huang a Chinese spy, an allegation that China denies. title: Analysts Set Nvidia (NVDA) Stock Price Target For 12 Months - TradingView
content: Even though Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ: NVDA) stock has capitulated by more than 27% over the past six consecutive weeks, Wall Street analysts are optimistic of a potential bull rally to a new all-time high (ATH) over the next 12 months. As of November 11, 2026, 35 Wall Street analysts surveyed by TipRanks over the past 3 months have set an average price target for Nvidia stock at $317.83. With NVDA trading at $175.87 at the time of reporting, these analysts signal a possible 80.72% upside over the next 12 months. These Wall Street analysts have issued an average ‘Strong Buy’ rating for Nvidia stock. Earlier on Wednesday, Atif Malik, an expert at Citigroup Inc. C reiterated a ‘Buy’ rating for NVDA. He, however, lowered his 12-month price target for Nvidia to $285 from $315. Tristan Gerra, a Wall Street analyst at Robert Baird, downgraded NVDA stock to ‘Hold’. Additionally, Gerra lowered his 12-month price target for the company to $200 from $500. Meanwhile, Joseph Moore, an analyst at Morgan Stanley MS reaffirmed a ‘Buy’ rating for NVDA and set a 12-month price target at $300. Despite Nvidia stock facing bearish sentiment catalyzed by the broader United States and China trade tensions, Wall Street analysts are expecting a possible bull run to a new ATH over the next 12 months. Furthermore, NVDA stock has retested a major 52-week support level at about $165 following the recent selloff. At the time of publication, the company had a market capitalization of roughly $4.07 trillion. Although the company is facing potential regulatory scrutiny over third-party supply-chain bypasses, Wall Street analysts are signaling another bull market fueled by the mainstream demand for artificial intelligence (AI). title: Nvidia Stock Just Had Its Price Target Slashed 60%. Others Still Say Buy. Who's Right? - The Motley Fool
content: Baird downgraded Nvidia on Wednesday and cut its price target to $200. Morgan Stanley still sees the stock reaching $300, and others also remain bullish. Here's what each side is betting on and what investors should watch next week. As uncertainty whirls around CEO Jensen Huang's blistering scandal, Wall Street can't agree on what Nvidia (NVDA +2.87%) is worth. On Wednesday morning, Baird downgraded the chipmaker to Neutral from Outperform and cut its price target by 60%, to $200 from $500. Within hours, Morgan Stanley took Nvidia off its list of top stock ideas but kept its Overweight rating and a $300 target. That leaves two respected firms about $100 a share apart on the world's most important AI company. The stock shrugged off both calls. Nvidia rose nearly 5% to about $177 by midday Wednesday as semiconductor stocks rallied after strong results from AI cloud company CoreWeave (CRWV +24.71%). Even so, Nvidia is still about 26% below its Oct. 6 record close of $239.24. Baird's concern isn't today's demand. Its analyst said lead times for Nvidia's newest chips remain stretched, with demand well exceeding supply. Instead, the worry is next year. Baird said it is pushing back its 2027 data center forecasts due to a recent lack of visibility. Supply problems are the main reason, but the firm also sees possible softening in demand because spending by the big cloud companies could grow by 40% or slightly less in 2027. Baird also said uncertainty about Huang's tenure supports a Neutral rating. Nvidia's board is investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, after he acknowledged an affair with an executive at a company that buys Nvidia hardware. Nvidia's own annual report warns that it is "highly dependent on the services of our long-standing executive team." When the Total Conviction signal flashed for Nvidia in 2009, most people ignored it. The ones who acted turned $5,000 into $2,799,718*. Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. Meanwhile, Morgan Stanley's move looks bigger than it is. The firm removed Nvidia from its top picks because of a rule that a top pick that falls more than 25% from the day it was named is automatically dropped. Nvidia was named on Oct. 2. Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore said there is no change to the firm's view of a strong and durable AI buildout, but he acknowledged that near-term uncertainty will persist as investors debate how crucial Huang is to Nvidia's direction. Wells Fargo also has a $300 price target on Nvidia. The bank gave a $15 trim to the target on Tuesday but said it expects Nvidia to report solid earnings that will help assuage investor concerns about the durability of the AI investment cycle. The latest numbers back up the bulls. In Nvidia's most recent quarter, revenue rose 106% to $96.2 billion, and data center sales reached $89 billion. The company guided for about $108 billion in revenue this quarter, even assuming no data center computing sales in China. Look closely, and the two firms aren't that far apart on the business. Both say demand is strong right now. Even Baird's cautious scenario has the largest customers increasing their AI spending by about 40% in 2027, which is a slowdown but still a lot of growth. The real gap is about how much to discount the stock for a possible supply crunch and the chance that Huang leaves. At about $177, Baird's $200 target implies roughly 13% upside. Morgan Stanley's $300 target implies about 70%. For long-term investors, the bull case looks better grounded in Nvidia's actual results, but the next week matters. Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Nov. 17, and investors should listen for a few things: whether its forecast for next quarter holds up, what management says about supply, and whether it addresses the board's investigation. If the numbers stay strong and the investigation clears Huang, today's price could look cheap in hindsight. But if guidance slips, Baird's caution will look smart. Either way, investors who own Nvidia should keep the position at a size they can live with because the swings in AI stocks surely aren't over. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. After the stock dropped 25%, two of Wall Street's biggest banks pulled it from their top-pick lists, and neither could bring itself to say "sell" — yet. Morgan Stanley's version was the most polite: It's not you, it's our stop-loss policy. The bank removes any top pick that falls more than 25% from where it was named, and Nvidia had slid a bit more since getting the title on Oct. 2. Only a day earlier, Bank of America cut Nvidia, Micron (MU) and Lam Research (LRCX) from its US 1 List of best ideas. Both banks still rate Nvidia a Buy. Others were less gentle. Baird cut the stock to Neutral on Wednesday and slashed its price target to $200 from $500, citing rising odds of a CEO change. Aletheia Capital downgraded Nvidia to Hold on Monday. Of 82 analysts who rate the stock, 77 call it a Buy, according to Bloomberg data. The average price target sits about 87% above where the stock closed Tuesday. Wall Street's reluctance to get bearish on Nvidia has history on its side, mostly. Nvidia has closed 25% below a record 13 times since its 1999 IPO. After drops in 2001, 2002, and 2007, the stock lost more than half its value again over the next 12 months. It's also a small sample, and half of it comes from the dot-com boom and bust, when Nvidia was a fraction of today's $4 trillion giant. title: Prediction: After Losing Over $1.7 Trillion in Market Cap This Year, Nvidia Stock Will Rebound in Epic Fashion. Here's Why. - The Motley Fool
content: For much of 2026, Nvidia (NVDA +2.87%) looked unstoppable. The artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker delivered strong financial results, while Wall Street rewarded its dominance with a lofty valuation. In early October, Nvidia's market capitalization peaked around $5.8 trillion, making it the world's most valuable company. Unfortunately, the momentum didn't last. As of this writing (Nov. 10), Nvidia's market cap has fallen to $4.1 trillion. That's a decline of 29%, representing roughly $1.7 trillion in lost value. The sell-off reflects growing uncertainty surrounding AI infrastructure spending, political developments, and a new investigation involving CEO Jensen Huang. Nevertheless, I think investors are overlooking something important. Nvidia's stock price has changed dramatically, but its underlying competitive advantages haven't disappeared. Here's why I think the semiconductor behemoth could stage a comeback in 2027. Nvidia's meteoric rise isn't simply the result of investors being excited about AI. It was actually supported by unprecedented growth in revenue and profit. During the company's fiscal second quarter, Nvidia generated $96.2 billion in revenue, representing a 106% increase year over year. The data center business contributed $89 billion, growing 117% annually, while earnings per share (EPS) surged 128% to $2.46. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $2,195,396 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. Nvidia's growth is an extension of the capital expenditure (capex) commitments from hyperscalers including Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta Platforms, and Oracle. As big tech expands its computing infrastructure to train and operate AI models, companies are purchasing Nvidia's GPUs, networking equipment, and integrated computing systems. The company's Blackwell architecture has been instrumental in meeting this demand, while the newer Vera Rubin platform is entering full-scale production. Nvidia is also expanding into specialized inference accelerators and agentic AI. In other words, Nvidia isn't simply selling individual chips. It's building a comprehensive stack of hardware and software for the next generation of AI. This explains why investors were willing to assign the company such a premium valuation. Nvidia's valuation increasingly depends on the assumption that AI infrastructure spending will continue expanding at an unprecedented pace. However, investors are beginning to question how quickly the hyperscalers can generate enough returns on their data center investments. The midterm elections introduced another layer of uncertainty. With Democrats gaining control of Congress, investors are reassessing the possibility of additional scrutiny surrounding data center construction, energy consumption, and electricity prices. While this doesn't mean AI spending will suddenly collapse, tighter regulations or slower project approvals could affect the timing of infrastructure investments. More recently, Nvidia has encountered an entirely different challenge. Reports concerning CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a business executive suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence prompted Nvidia's board of directors to launch an investigation. While the board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security information were compromised, the situation introduces governance and potential succession risks. If Huang is eventually replaced or steps down as CEO, investors would understandably question how the transition might affect Nvidia's strategy, customer relationships, and execution. For now, the uncertainty itself is contributing to outsize pressure on Nvidia shares. Despite these challenges, I think Nvidia remains exceptionally well positioned for long-term growth. Consider the company's competitive position. Advanced Micro Devices is expanding its AI accelerator business, while Broadcom is helping companies develop custom chips. However, neither competitor has replicated Nvidia's ecosystem of GPUs, networking technology, and the CUDA software system. This ecosystem matters because it makes switching suppliers considerably time-consuming and expensive, creating meaningful barriers to competition. Even if data center construction slows, that doesn't necessarily mean Nvidia's existing customers will stop purchasing the company's products. Cloud providers and frontier labs will still need to continue upgrading infrastructure, replacing older systems, and supporting growing demand for AI inference. Even if Nvidia eventually operates under a different CEO, the company's technology, intellectual property (IP), customer relationships, and engineering talent aren't going to vanish overnight. Likewise, slower growth in AI infrastructure spending doesn't automatically eliminate Nvidia's profitability. Nvidia could look different a year from now. Its leadership might change, its customers could become more selective, and its growth rate might moderate. Nevertheless, I expect Nvidia to remain one of the most important and profitable companies in the AI industry. In the short term, stock prices are often driven by sentiment, uncertainty, and headlines. Over the long term, earnings growth and valuation tend to matter far more. That's why I think Nvidia's recent sell-off could look like a compelling buying opportunity, and why I'm predicting a meaningful recovery in 2027. The stock closed at $162.88 on July 9, 2025, and went on to gain as much as 44.7% within a year. From $167.02 on September 5, 2025, its best gain was 41.1%. Both gains ran to the same closing high, $235.74. Neither of those two dates is among the five visits counted below, which use a different test: a visit counts only when the stock falls to within 5% of today’s price from above, at least 21 trading days after the one before. The stock fell back to this price five times in the two years to November 10, 2026. Two of those visits went on to rise 20% before falling 5%, and three fell 5% first. Those three slides all reached 5% down in late March 2026. Yet a visit on March 20, 2026 went on to rise 20% by April 24. If bought today, $10,000 of NVIDIA stock would be worth $12,420 if it climbed back to resistance, the price where two earlier rallies stalled. If it matched the typical gain of the two 2025 rallies, the same $10,000 would become $14,290. The stock would thus need a smaller rise to reach resistance than those rallies delivered. Two lower levels, at $185.55 and $192.54, stand in the way first. Yet most recent visits to this price slid first, and NVIDIA’s sales growth over the past twelve months is below its own three-year average. NVIDIA’s sales growth has sped up for four straight quarters, but management expects its gross margin to slip. Year-on-year revenue growth rose from 73.2% in fiscal Q4 2026 to 85.2% in fiscal Q1 2027. Revenue of $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2 2027 was up 105.9% from a year earlier. Over the twelve months to July 26, 2026, though, revenue grew 83.4%, under the 116.5% average of NVIDIA’s last three twelve-month periods, which include 194.7% growth in the year to July 2024. For fiscal Q3 2027, management guided revenue to $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, with its new Vera Rubin systems about 20% of data center revenue. Data center revenue was $89 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, up 18% from the quarter before, management said. Gross margin is where NVIDIA is weaker. It was 75% in fiscal Q2 2027. On the August 26, 2026 call, management said memory prices had risen more than it expected, and it guided gross margin to 74%, plus or minus 50 basis points, for fiscal Q3 2027. It expects margins to bottom in fiscal Q4 2027 in the 71% to 72% range before settling at 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028, as price increases take effect. The risk is a fall below $160.45, where support counts as broken. NVIDIA’s profits could suffer from the lower gross margin, and management expects supply to remain a bottleneck at least through the end of fiscal 2028. If support does break, the next support below is $128.91, which is 23.7% under today’s price. NVIDIA stock has bounced from this price before, and its sales growth has kept speeding up through the latest quarter. But management expects gross margin to keep falling through fiscal Q4 2027. NVIDIA’s fiscal Q3 2027 gross margin, against management’s 74% guide, is the number to watch when the company reports in November 2026. title: What Just Happened To Nvidia Stock? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Nvidia (NVDA) stock fell 5.5% on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.4%. The decline occurred a day after a securities class action lawsuit was filed against the company on November 9, and on the day its independent directors released a statement. What did the board say, and what does the lawsuit seek? Nvidia’s Board Retains A Former Acting U.S. Attorney On November 10, the independent members of Nvidia’s board said they had retained a former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York. The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, was brought on behalf of investors who bought Nvidia shares from October 2025 to early November 2026. It seeks to recover damages for those investors under federal securities laws. Nvidia stock had already lost 4.3% on the day the suit was filed, which made Tuesday’s drop its second loss in a row. Most did not. Three of the five companies on Nvidia’s peer list rose on November 10, with Broadcom up 3.9%, while Intel fell 2.1%. The wider market was softer. A hot October inflation report weighed on markets that day, and Deutsche Bank said it expects the Fed to raise rates in January 2027 after that data. The S&P 500 edged lower and the technology sector fund, XLK, fell 1.2%. Nvidia’s fall was far larger than either, and no peer fell as much, so the drop was mostly Nvidia’s own. Declines of this size are rare for Nvidia. Only two sessions in the prior year brought a drop at least this big, the latest on November 5, when the stock lost 9.3%. Over twelve months the stock is down 10.0%, while the S&P 500 returned 13.1%. Shares closed Tuesday at $168.89, just above their 52-week closing low of $165.17 on March 30, 2026. title: Nvidia (NVDA) Q3 earnings preview: AI spending risks and governance concerns threaten major uptrend - MarketPulse
content: Ahead of next Tuesday’s Q3 FY2027 earnings, Nvidia (NVDA) faces a critical test of investor confidence as concerns over the sustainability of the AI infrastructure spending boom are now compounded by an emerging corporate governance controversy involving CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia’s shares fell 4.3% on Monday, 9 November 2026, wiping approximately US$190 billion off its market capitalisation, following reports of an investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by an alleged Chinese intelligence operation. The development has added a new layer of uncertainty to the company’s leadership, US-China regulatory exposure and elevated valuation. Overall, the most valuable company in the world is now facing a double whammy of macro and micro headwinds that led to a significant decline of almost 30% in Nvidia’s market capitalisation in a span of less than one month, from a peak of US$5.77 trillion on 6 October 2026 to US$4.07 trillion on Tuesday, 10 November 2026. The AI juggernaut is scheduled to release its results at approximately 4:20 pm US Eastern Time on Tuesday, 17 November 2026, followed by its earnings conference call at 5 pm ET (6 am Singapore time on Wednesday, 18 November 2026). Based on the street’s consensus, revenue and earnings growth are expected to be rosy: revenue is expected to increase a whopping 90.9% year-on-year to US$108.84 billion, while EPS is expected to skyrocket 90% year-on-year to US$2.47. Ahead of Nvidia’s Q3 FY2027 earnings release, options markets are pricing an approximately ±10.6% move in Nvidia’s shares (NVDA) as of 10 November 2026, above its 10-year average peak earnings-day movement of ±7.8%, according to data from EarningsWatcher. Nvidia’s upcoming earnings could have significant implications for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100, given its substantial index weighting and increasingly interconnected financial relationships across the US artificial intelligence ecosystem. Nvidia accounted for approximately 8.18% of the Nasdaq 100 as of 20 October 2026, meaning a 5% movement in its shares alone could move the index by roughly 0.41 percentage points, assuming other constituents remain unchanged. More importantly, growing concerns over circular financing, where Nvidia invests in, provides financing support to, or guarantees obligations involving AI infrastructure companies that subsequently purchase its chips, have raised questions about the independence and sustainability of AI-related demand. In August, Nvidia announced a financing initiative targeting more than US$500 billion in third-party capital, with potential company-backed guarantees of up to US$125 billion. These arrangements could amplify contagion risks: a slowdown in AI demand or tightening credit conditions could weaken data-centre operators’ cash flows, restrict their ability to finance new chip purchases and ultimately weigh on Nvidia’s future revenue growth. Such a development could trigger simultaneous selling across semiconductor manufacturers, hyperscalers, AI infrastructure providers and private-credit-exposed financial institutions. Consequently, a stronger-than-expected Nvidia earnings beat, and robust forward guidance could restore confidence in the broader AI investment cycle, while disappointing results or signs of weakening end-user demand could accelerate the recent sell-off in the Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500. Let’s now focus on the six key fundamental factors traders should monitor. Nvidia’s Data Centre division remains the dominant earnings engine, supported by massive AI infrastructure investment from hyperscalers, cloud service providers and sovereign AI projects. In Q2 FY2027, Data Centre revenue surged 117% year on year to US$89.0 billion, accounting for approximately 92.5% of total revenue. Overall Q2 revenue reached US$96.2 billion, up 106% year on year. For Q3, management previously guided to total revenue of US$108 billion, plus or minus 2%, while consensus expectations have risen to approximately US$108.8 billion. The critical issue is whether the company can continue delivering substantial sequential growth as its revenue base expands. Nvidia’s ability to maintain its dominant position in AI accelerators depends heavily on the successful deployment of its Blackwell architecture and next-generation Vera Rubin platform. In its Q2 results, management confirmed that Vera Rubin had entered full production, with deployments progressing across major cloud partners including Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and CoreWeave. Traders will focus on production capacity, customer deployment schedules, advanced packaging, and the availability of high-bandwidth memory, alongside competition from AMD and hyperscalers’ internally developed AI chips. Nvidia’s Q2 non-GAAP gross margin remained at 75%, reflecting its exceptional pricing power within the AI accelerator market. However, management guided Q3 gross margin lower to 74%, plus or minus 50 basis points, as higher manufacturing, packaging and memory costs potentially weigh on profitability. With quarterly revenue expected to exceed US$108 billion, even a relatively small change in gross margin can translate into a substantial difference in operating profit. Traders will assess whether Nvidia can offset rising infrastructure component costs through higher selling prices, product mix and manufacturing efficiencies. Nvidia’s earnings reaction will likely depend more on its Q4 FY2027 revenue outlook than its reported Q3 performance. The market will be looking for confirmation that AI infrastructure orders remain resilient into early 2027, particularly after recent concerns over hyperscaler capital expenditure, AI financing arrangements and the profitability of large-scale AI deployments. Nvidia has also announced partnerships involving Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR intended to mobilise substantial third-party capital for AI infrastructure development, subject to definitive agreements.8 While these arrangements could broaden financing capacity, investors will scrutinise whether AI infrastructure spending is supported by sustainable end-user demand and cash generation. China remains both a substantial potential market and a major source of regulatory uncertainty for Nvidia. Importantly, its Q3 revenue guidance assumes no Data Centre compute revenue from China, reflecting existing restrictions and uncertainties surrounding advanced AI chip exports. Traders will focus on whether Nvidia can improve its access to Chinese customers, obtain additional export approvals or face tighter restrictions. This factor is particularly important, given that Nvidia’s proprietary CUDA software ecosystem and its position in the global AI accelerator market depend in part on the breadth of its international customer base. This is the most significant new non-earnings catalyst heading into Nvidia’s Q3 announcement. According to Reuters reports published on 8–9 November, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after allegations that Jensen Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom US intelligence officials reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. From an equity valuation perspective, the greater concern is that the investigation could create a prolonged governance discount, especially if it introduces uncertainty over leadership continuity, US export approvals or regulatory compliance. More importantly, the development coincides with a period of heightened investor scepticism towards the broader AI trade, amplifying the risk of a negative reaction to any earnings disappointment. Also, any evidence of a security breach, regulatory enforcement action, leadership disruption or additional material disclosures could trigger a sustained valuation derating, even if the company delivers strong earnings. Nvidia’s Q3 earnings reaction will likely hinge on five key factors: Data Centre revenue growth, Blackwell/Rubin execution, gross margin resilience, Q4 guidance and the implications of the Jensen Huang investigation, with the sustainability of hyperscaler AI spending remaining the overarching fundamental driver. The bull case is clean earnings beat, accelerating AI infrastructure demand, stronger-than-expected Q4 guidance and resilient gross margins, accompanied by reassuring developments on the corporate governance investigation. This combination could trigger a sharp recovery in Nvidia’s shares and potentially restore confidence across the wider semiconductor and AI-related technology sectors. The bear case is not necessarily disappointing headline earnings, but evidence that AI infrastructure spending is losing momentum or that higher costs are beginning to erode profitability. More importantly, any material escalation in the investigation, particularly involving regulatory enforcement, confirmed security breaches or leadership disruption, could introduce a prolonged governance discount even if Nvidia’s underlying earnings remain strong. Here’s the charting corner as we dissect NVDA’s multi-week and multi-month outlook from a technical analysis perspective. The price action of NVDA has staged a bearish breakdown on 30 October 2026 from the 200-day moving average and the “Ascending Wedge” support, following the formation of a major bearish reversal “Ascending Wedge” configuration from the 7 April 2025 low of 86.60 to the current all-time high of 243.37 printed on 6 October 2026 (see Fig. 1). In addition, the Chaikin Money Flow indicator, a combination of price and volume momentum, has continued to exhibit a bearish momentum condition below the zero centreline. The volatility-adjusted relative strength (VARS) of NVDA, measured against the broader S&P 500 exchange-traded fund (SPY), continues to show NVDA’s underperformance. All in all, these observations suggest that NVDA is in a potential major downtrend phase below the 201.66 key medium-term pivotal resistance (also the 200-day moving average). A break below 152.90, the intermediate support, exposes the medium-term support at 129.16 (also the long-term secular ascending trendline running from the 13 October 2022 low) in the first step. On the flip side, a clearance and a daily close above 201.66 would invalidate the bearish scenario, opening the door to a potential recovery towards the medium-term resistance at 220.00 (also the 50-day moving average). We just published a list of the 10 Stocks Analysts Just Downgraded and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) ranked 10th on this list. Wall Street has had a rough start to November. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% on November 5, its steepest one-day drop in 19 months, and slid into a correction, more than 10% below its October 6 record close. The semiconductor index lost more than 12% that day, and about $3 trillion in value was erased from S&P 500 companies. Fear of tighter rules on AI drove much of the rout. Democratic wins in the November elections raised concerns that stricter regulation could slow the buildout of AI infrastructure, and the stocks tied to data centers took the hardest hit. Investors who had been paying up for AI growth suddenly had to ask how much of that growth could be stopped by politics. Not everyone saw the drop as a verdict on the AI trade. Jed Ellerbroek of Argent Capital Management described the selling as a capitulation phase for data center beneficiaries, meaning forced selling that often marks a low. A Wall Street research shop, Yardeni, argued that political pushback on data centers amounts to "speed bumps, not roadblocks, even though Wall Street seems to be pricing in the latter." The economy did not offer a cushion. Payrolls rose by 165,000 in October, far above the 65,000 to 70,000 economists expected, and the unemployment rate stood at 4.1%. That kept a December rate hike in play, and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin have both hinted that higher rates could be on the table. On Monday, strategists led by Beata Manthey cut US stocks and the global technology sector to neutral and raised European stocks outside the UK to overweight. Manthey warned that positioning in stocks "could reset lower into net-short territory." The S&P 500 had its biggest weekly loss since April 2025, which helps explain why many investors are looking for cheaper places to put money. You might also be interested in our list of affordable stocks Wall Street analysts like. Stocks bounced back on Monday. His worry is not demand for the chips but the money Nvidia has promised to the companies buying them. Chang said an AI Computing Partner program has pushed the company's financial commitments up more than tenfold, to $165 billion in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, and he called the funding picture for smaller AI cloud builders opaque. He also pointed to a guarantee the company gave on an Ohio data center. Nvidia designs the chips that run most large AI data centers, and the business behind the worry is still growing fast. Revenue came in at $96.2 billion last quarter, up 106% from a year earlier, and Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said the AI infrastructure buildout is "at full steam." The earnings report, which is expected to be released on November 17, might help the stock move higher if these key numbers are better than expectations. On the other hand, if they miss, the stock may move lower. While the sustainability of the immediate price change and future earnings expectations will mostly depend on management's discussion of business conditions on the earnings call, it's worth handicapping the probability of a positive EPS surprise. This maker of graphics chips for gaming and artificial intelligence is expected to post quarterly earnings of $2.49 per share in its upcoming report, which represents a year-over-year change of +91.5%. Revenues are expected to be $108.99 billion, up 91.2% from the year-ago quarter. The consensus EPS estimate for the quarter has been revised 0.61% higher over the last 30 days to the current level. This is essentially a reflection of how the covering analysts have collectively reassessed their initial estimates over this period. Investors should keep in mind that the direction of estimate revisions by each of the covering analysts may not always get reflected in the aggregate change. Estimate revisions ahead of a company's earnings release offer clues to the business conditions for the period whose results are coming out. Our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction) -- has this insight at its core. title: Nvidia sells off for second day in fallout from Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged spy - CNBC
content:
Nvidia shares sank 5.47% on Tuesday as investors continued to weigh the potential fallout from CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The embattled chip giant briefly dipped below $4 trillion in market cap during afternoon trading, but bounced back to close above that level. Nvidia last cleared the $4 trillion benchmark on July 9, 2025. Shares closed more than 4% lower on Monday, the day after Huang told staff in an email that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife and had "fallen short" of his responsibilities as CEO. He reportedly had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. The New York Times on Oct. 29 reported that U.S. officials had concluded she was "a Chinese intelligence asset, funneling information to Beijing" and "possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China." U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI is investigating. "I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time, but not too long ago," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We'll look into it. I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape." Adding to the tech giant's woes was a class-action shareholder lawsuit filed against Nvidia and Huang in federal court in San Jose, California. The Rosen Law Firm's suit alleges the defendants made false or misleading statements about his affair with Huang and Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed, thereby presenting a material risk to the company's reputation and business prospects. "Right now the Street and investor chatter is assigning roughly a 15% chance he is removed as CEO of Nvidia with a high probability (85%) he stays on as CEO after the Board investigation is completed," said Dan Ives, senior and managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co, in a Tuesday note. "We would expect a Board investigation that could take 4 weeks to 6 weeks and will create a clear overhand on the stock until more news emerges from Nvidia." Amid Nvidia's turmoil, some of its chip rivals are seeing a boost. Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom built on a strong start to the week, with AMD gaining 1.3% and Broadcom adding nearly 4%. AMD gained 13% on Monday, while Broadcom added just over 10%. — CNBC's Dan Mangan and Caleigh Keating contributed to this report. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. The artificial intelligence (AI) computing giant remains about 22% below its 52-week high after Friday's premarket rebound. Yet CEO Jensen Huang reminded us just two weeks ago that "Demand is extraordinary. Capacity is the constraint." That hardly describes a business losing any momentum. I believe political uncertainty deserves attention, but recent deployments suggest the global buildout continues. Nvidia held about $32 billion of inventory while preparing for Rubin's launch. Converting that investment into system deliveries could help revenue beat guidance. Production shipments began during Q3, and management expects Rubin to contribute about 20% of quarterly Data Center revenue. We are also looking at Neoclouds expanding to serve enterprises and sovereign customers. Management expects those buyers to drive sequential growth, with hyperscaler growth reaccelerating afterward as Rubin supply improves. I'll be watching shipment conversion closely because customers can't generate revenue until Nvidia delivers the equipment. Gross margins need attention too. Management expects 74% in Q3, down from 75%, as memory costs surge. Q4 could fall to 71%–72%. Those remain exceptional margins, and higher volumes can support earnings despite the pressure. Guidance also assumes no China Data Center compute revenue. Any permitted sales could help, although I wouldn't rely on them. Now, I believe Nvidia's growth will extend beyond this upcoming quarter. Several recent announcements point in that direction. Oracle's (ORCL) October 27 expansion targets multi-gigawatt Vera Rubin infrastructure. Google's (GOOGL) A5X infrastructure is designed to scale to 960,000 Rubin graphics processing units (GPUs) across multiple sites, with general availability planned this month. These are long-term deployment plans. Meanwhile, Meta (META) is expanding Rubin and Vera central processing unit (CPU) deployments around Muse. Those plans support demand beyond training. Running agents and improving models through reinforcement learning require substantial compute. Physical AI also adds robotics workloads. Nvidia also captures spending on networking and CPUs alongside GPUs, while Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) supports customers across hardware generations. The physical rollout should improve too. DSX POD modular factories can be installed in as little as 14 days, with deliveries planned for early 2027. That applies to prepared sites with supporting infrastructure. Of course, it doesn't eliminate permitting or power requirements. Still, faster installation helps turn spending into usable capacity. Management expects roughly 70% Fiscal 2028 revenue growth, with supply constrained through that year. It's also worth mentioning that October's capacity agreements target a 2.5x substrate expansion over three years. Manufacturing partners are making long-term commitments to meet Nvidia's requirements. Expansion is increasingly global. Google is adding European availability, while Saudi Arabia's HUMAIN plans further Blackwell and Rubin deployments. I believe this gives Nvidia customers outside the U.S. a construction cycle. Now, to be fair, the Democratic congressional sweep has intensified regulatory fears. This is especially true around electricity costs and development restrictions. However, Congress generally doesn't approve individual data centers. Zoning decisions usually sit locally, while environmental permitting and grid connections involve separate authorities. State leadership therefore matters. So, sure, Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa wants development paused pending protections, and local ballot measures favored restrictions. Delays could hurt deliveries, including contracted projects. However, I think markets are assuming too much demand disappears. Developers can relocate projects, although that takes time. Meta's Prometheus first phase is already complete. Existing infrastructure and international projects leave considerable demand moving forward. Nvidia's valuation looks increasingly attractive after the recent sell-off. At today's price, Fiscal 2027 consensus EPS of $9.31 implies 20.04x earnings. Fiscal 2028's $15.91 estimate brings that to roughly 12x. Forecasts of $21.34 for Fiscal 2029 and $25.98 for Fiscal 2030 imply 8.74x and 7.19x. Expected EPS growth slows from roughly 95% this year to 71%, then 34% and 22%. Those are demanding forecasts, especially further out. Nevertheless, even, say, a 30% shortfall against Fiscal 2028 consensus leaves $11.14 EPS and a 17.1x multiple. Of course, such a misstep is highly unlikely. Regardless, I find even that multiple reasonable for Nvidia's competitive position. Its net-cash balance sheet supports continued investment. CUDA and its networking platform help customers deploy whole systems efficiently. Earnings growth can support returns without a higher multiple. Better shipment execution could also raise estimates. In any case, there are a number of risks to keep in mind. Hyperscalers could moderate capex if AI returns disappoint. Google and Amazon's (AMZN) custom accelerators threaten some workloads, while AMD (AMD) competes for customers. Memory inflation could exceed current assumptions. Nvidia's enormous expected scale also makes shares sensitive to any disappointment. A strong quarter alone cannot remove those risks. Nvidia stock has a Strong Buy consensus, based on 33 Buy ratings. The average price target of $323.45 implies 73% upside from today's share price. I remain bullish ahead of Q3. Political obstacles can slow construction, but customer deployments suggest the compute shortage persists. Around 12x Fiscal 2028 earnings looks unusually attractive to me. Nvidia can deliver compelling returns through earnings growth, provided customers keep converting their AI ambitions into operating capacity.
